questions.stem: Which prediction of classical mechanics fails for objects moving at speeds approaching the speed of light?
options: Velocities simply add, so light from a moving source should travel faster than c
An object at rest stays at rest unless an unbalanced force acts on the object
Total momentum is conserved when two objects collide in an isolated system
An object moving in a circle at constant speed accelerates towards the centre
questions.explanation: Classical mechanics adds velocities directly, so it predicts light from a fast source would exceed c, and that a large enough force could push any object past c. Both fail near c. The first law, conservation of momentum and centripetal acceleration all still hold in special relativity.

questions.stem: Einstein’s first postulate of special relativity states that:
options: time passes at the same rate in every frame of reference
there is one absolute frame of reference, defined by the aether
the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames of reference
the laws of physics are the same in all accelerating frames of reference
questions.explanation: The first postulate says no experiment can single out one inertial (non-accelerating) frame as being truly at rest, because the laws of physics are identical in all of them. Special relativity deals only with inertial frames, and it denies an absolute frame such as the aether.

questions.stem: An inertial frame of reference is one that is:
options: moving in a circle at constant speed
not accelerating
accelerating at a constant rate
rotating at a constant rate
questions.explanation: An inertial frame moves at constant velocity, so Newton’s first law holds in it. Rotating and circular motion both involve acceleration, even at constant speed, because the direction of the velocity keeps changing.

questions.stem: A spacecraft moving towards Earth at 0.50c sends a light pulse ahead of it. At what speed does an observer on Earth measure the pulse to travel?
options: c
questions.explanation: Einstein’s second postulate says the speed of light is the same for all observers, whatever the motion of the source. Adding the velocities, as classical physics does, gives 1.5c, which no observer ever measures.

questions.stem: A passenger in a train moving smoothly at constant velocity drops a ball. How do the laws of motion inside the train compare with those on the station platform?
options: They are different, because the ball drifts towards the back of the train
They are different, because a moving train is not an inertial frame
They are identical only while the train is moving slowly enough
They are identical, so no experiment inside can show that the train is moving
questions.explanation: A train moving at constant velocity is an inertial frame, so by the first postulate the laws of physics are the same inside it as on the platform. The ball falls straight down relative to the passenger. This holds at any constant speed, not just low ones.

questions.stem: What did Michelson and Morley expect their interferometer to detect?
options: The time dilation of light travelling along their interferometer arms
A change in the speed of light caused by Earth’s motion through the aether
A change in the frequency of light caused by the rotation of Earth
The length contraction of the arms of their apparatus as Earth moved
questions.explanation: Physicists then thought light travelled through a medium, the aether. Earth’s motion through it should make light’s speed differ along different directions, shifting the interference pattern as the apparatus turned. Length contraction and time dilation had not yet been proposed.

questions.stem: The Michelson–Morley experiment found no shift in the interference pattern as the apparatus was rotated. How is this null result interpreted?
options: It showed that light needs the aether as a medium in order to travel
It gave no evidence of an aether, consistent with light’s speed being constant
It showed that light travels faster in the direction of Earth’s orbital motion
It measured Earth’s speed through the aether to a high level of accuracy
questions.explanation: No shift meant no detectable difference in light’s speed in different directions, so there was no evidence for the aether. That is consistent with Einstein’s postulate that the speed of light is the same for all observers. A shift would have been needed to measure any speed through the aether.

questions.stem: Which statement is true in special relativity but not in classical physics?
options: Observers in relative motion always agree on the length of a moving rod
Velocities always add directly, however large they are
Time passes at the same rate in every frame of reference
Observers in relative motion can disagree about the time between two events
questions.explanation: In special relativity, time intervals and lengths depend on the observer’s frame: moving clocks run slow and moving objects are contracted. Classical physics treats time and length as absolute and adds velocities directly, which is why the other statements belong to classical physics.

questions.stem: Why are relativistic effects not noticed at everyday speeds, such as a jet flying at 300 m s⁻¹?
options: γ is exactly 1 until the speed is more than half the speed of light
Relativistic effects only happen in frames that are accelerating
γ is extremely close to 1, so the dilation and contraction are tiny
Relativistic effects apply only to light, never to moving matter
questions.explanation: At 300 m s⁻¹, v/c is 10⁻⁶, so γ differs from 1 by only about 5 × 10⁻¹³. The effects are real but far too small to notice without atomic clocks. γ rises smoothly above 1 at every speed; there is no threshold.

questions.stem: Proper time is the time interval between two events measured:
options: in the frame in which both events occur at the same place
by any observer who is at rest on the surface of Earth
in the frame that is moving fastest relative to the events
in the frame in which the two events are furthest apart
questions.explanation: Proper time, t₀, is measured by a clock present at both events, which is possible only in the frame where they happen at the same point. Observers in every other frame measure a longer, dilated interval. Being on Earth does not make a frame special.

questions.stem: The proper length of an object is its length measured:
options: in the frame in which the object is at rest
by an observer moving at close to the speed of light
in the frame of an observer standing on Earth
while the object moves at its greatest speed
questions.explanation: Proper length, L₀, is measured in the object’s rest frame and is the longest length any observer measures. Observers moving relative to the object measure it contracted along the direction of motion.

questions.stem: An astronaut on a spacecraft moving at 0.60c relative to Earth times her own heartbeats. Observers on Earth also time them. Who measures the proper time between beats?
options: The astronaut, because the beats happen at one place in her frame
The Earth observers, because Earth is the frame at rest
Both, because each of them is in an inertial frame
Neither, because both of the frames are in motion
questions.explanation: The heartbeats occur at the same point in the astronaut’s frame, so she measures the proper time. On Earth, successive beats happen at different places, so Earth observers measure a dilated, longer interval. No frame is absolutely at rest.

questions.stem: A spaceship flies past Earth at 0.80c. An astronaut on board and an observer on Earth both measure the ship’s length. Which statement is correct?
options: The Earth observer measures the proper length, which is the longer of the two
Both measure the same length, because a length does not depend on the frame
The astronaut measures the proper length, which is the shorter of the two
The astronaut measures the proper length, which is the longer of the two
questions.explanation: The ship is at rest relative to the astronaut, so she measures its proper length, L₀. The Earth observer sees the ship moving and measures it contracted along its motion, L = L₀/γ, which is shorter.

questions.stem: As an object’s speed approaches the speed of light, what happens to its Lorentz factor γ?
options: It approaches 2
It increases without limit
It approaches 1
It approaches 0
questions.explanation: γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²). As v approaches c, the denominator approaches zero, so γ grows without limit. γ is 1 at rest and is never less than 1.

questions.stem: What is the Lorentz factor γ for an object moving at 0.60c?
questions.explanation: γ = 1/√(1 − 0.60²) = 1/√0.64 = 1/0.80 = 1.25. 0.80 is the square root before inverting, and 1.56 forgets the square root. 1.67 is γ for 0.80c.

questions.stem: An unstable particle has a lifetime of 2.0 µs in its own rest frame. In a laboratory it moves at 0.80c, where γ = 1.67. What lifetime is measured in the laboratory?
options: 3.3 µs
1.2 µs
2.0 µs
1.6 µs
questions.explanation: The particle’s own lifetime is the proper time, t₀. The laboratory measures the dilated time t = γt₀ = 1.67 × 2.0 ≈ 3.3 µs. Dividing by γ gives 1.2 µs, which would make moving clocks run fast.

questions.stem: A spacecraft has a proper length of 120 m. What length does an observer measure as it passes at 0.60c, where γ = 1.25?
questions.explanation: The observer sees the craft moving, so its length is contracted: L = L₀/γ = 120/1.25 = 96 m. Multiplying by γ gives 150 m, which treats the moving length as the longer one.

questions.stem: A square plate measures 1.0 m by 1.0 m in its rest frame. It moves past an observer at 0.866c, where γ = 2.0, parallel to one pair of its edges. What dimensions does the observer measure?
options: 0.50 m along the motion and 0.50 m across it
2.0 m along the motion and 1.0 m across it
1.0 m along the motion and 0.50 m across it
0.50 m along the motion and 1.0 m across it
questions.explanation: Length contraction happens only along the direction of motion: L = 1.0/2.0 = 0.50 m. Dimensions perpendicular to the motion are unchanged, so the width across stays 1.0 m. Contracting both edges is a common slip.

questions.stem: A spacecraft travels at 0.60c (γ = 1.25) to a star 6.0 light-years from Earth, as measured from Earth. How long does the trip take according to Earth clocks and according to the ship’s clock?
options: 10 years on Earth clocks and 8.0 years on the ship’s clock
10 years on Earth clocks and 12.5 years on the ship’s clock
8.0 years on Earth clocks and 10 years on the ship’s clock
6.0 years on Earth clocks and 4.8 years on the ship’s clock
questions.explanation: On Earth, time = 6.0 ly ÷ 0.60c = 10 years. The ship’s clock is present at both departure and arrival, so it records proper time: 10/1.25 = 8.0 years. The traveller’s clock records less time, not more.

questions.stem: A star is 8.0 light-years from Earth in Earth’s frame. A spacecraft travels to it at 0.80c, where γ = 1.67. How far is the journey in the spacecraft’s frame?
options: 8.0 light-years
6.4 light-years
4.8 light-years
13 light-years
questions.explanation: The Earth–star distance is a proper length in Earth’s frame. In the ship’s frame that distance moves past and is contracted: 8.0/1.67 ≈ 4.8 light-years. Multiplying by γ gives 13 light-years, which treats the moving length as longer.

questions.stem: From a spacecraft moving at constant high speed relative to Earth, how do Earth’s clocks appear to run, compared with the clocks on the spacecraft?
options: Slow, because Earth is moving relative to the spacecraft
Fast, because the spacecraft’s own clocks are running slow
At the same rate, because Earth itself is not moving
Fast, because Earth’s frame is the frame of proper time
questions.explanation: Time dilation is symmetrical between inertial frames: each observer measures the other’s clocks running slow. From the spacecraft, Earth is the moving frame, so Earth’s clocks appear slow. Neither frame is absolutely at rest.

questions.stem: Two spacecraft approach each other, each moving at 0.60c relative to Earth. What speed does one spacecraft measure for the other?
options: Less than c
Exactly c
questions.explanation: No observer measures any object moving faster than c, so the classical sum of 1.2c is impossible. The relativistic result is about 0.88c, which is less than c but more than 0.60c. Only light itself travels at exactly c.

questions.stem: Muons created about 15 km up in the atmosphere reach Earth’s surface, though their half-life suggests most should decay first. How is this explained in the muons’ own frame?
options: The distance to the surface is length-contracted, so it is short
Their half-life is time-dilated, as measured by their own clock
They travel faster than light relative to the atmosphere
The atmosphere is stretched, so its thickness is dilated
questions.explanation: In the muons’ frame their own half-life is the proper time and is not dilated. Instead, the atmosphere rushes past them and its thickness is contracted, so they cover it before decaying. Earth observers explain the same result with time dilation of the muons’ half-life.

questions.stem: Muons with a proper half-life of 1.5 µs travel through the atmosphere at 0.995c, where γ = 10. In Earth’s frame, how far does a muon travel in one half-life?
options: 4.5 km
45 km
questions.explanation: In Earth’s frame the half-life is dilated to γt₀ = 10 × 1.5 = 15 µs, so the distance is 0.995 × 3.0 × 10⁸ × 15 × 10⁻⁶ ≈ 4.5 km. Without time dilation the answer is only 0.45 km, which is why classical physics predicts that so few muons reach the ground.

questions.stem: Why must the time signals from GPS satellites be corrected for special relativity?
options: Light from a moving satellite reaches Earth at c plus the satellite’s speed
Their orbital speed contracts their signals’ wavelength to nearly nothing
Their orbital speed makes their clocks run slow compared with clocks on Earth
Their orbital speed makes their clocks run fast compared with clocks on Earth
questions.explanation: GPS satellites move at nearly 4 km s⁻¹, so in Earth’s frame their clocks are time-dilated and run slow by several microseconds a day. Positions depend on precise timing, so uncorrected errors would build up quickly. The signals still travel at c, as the second postulate requires.

questions.stem: Near the end of a 3.2 km linear accelerator, electrons have γ = 4.0 × 10⁴. How long is the accelerator in the electrons’ frame?
options: 8.0 cm
3.2 km
questions.explanation: In the electrons’ frame the accelerator moves past them and is length-contracted: L = L₀/γ = 3200/4.0 × 10⁴ = 0.080 m = 8.0 cm. Multiplying by γ instead gives 1.3 × 10⁸ m. Designers must use relativity like this, because classical calculations of the electrons’ motion fail near c.

questions.stem: What is the total energy of a particle of rest mass m moving with Lorentz factor γ?
options: γmc², its rest energy plus its kinetic energy
mc², whatever its speed happens to be
½mv², its kinetic energy alone at that speed
(γ − 1)mc², its rest energy alone at that speed
questions.explanation: Total energy is Etot = γmc² = Ek + E₀, where E₀ = mc² is the rest energy. The kinetic energy alone is (γ − 1)mc², which is the difference between total and rest energy, not the rest energy itself.

questions.stem: What is the rest energy of a 1.0 g mass? Use c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
questions.explanation: E₀ = mc² = 1.0 × 10⁻³ × (3.0 × 10⁸)² = 9.0 × 10¹³ J. Leaving the mass as 1.0 kg gives 9.0 × 10¹⁶ J, and forgetting to square c gives 3.0 × 10⁵ J.

questions.stem: An electron, with a rest energy of 8.2 × 10⁻¹⁴ J, moves with γ = 3.0. What is its kinetic energy?
questions.explanation: Ek = (γ − 1)mc² = 2.0 × 8.2 × 10⁻¹⁴ ≈ 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ J. γmc² gives 2.5 × 10⁻¹³ J, the total energy, and the classical ½mv² at this speed gives only 3.6 × 10⁻¹⁴ J, far too little.

questions.stem: Why does Ek = ½mv² give a value far too small for the kinetic energy of an electron moving at 0.9c?
options: The electron’s mass falls as it speeds up, so the true energy is even larger
The electron’s speed is length-contracted, so the v in the formula is too small
Kinetic energy is really γmc², which also includes the electron’s rest energy
Kinetic energy is really (γ − 1)mc², which grows without limit as v nears c
questions.explanation: The correct kinetic energy is (γ − 1)mc². At low speeds this matches ½mv², but as v nears c, γ rises steeply while ½mv² stays below ½mc². γmc² is the total energy, which includes the rest energy, so it is not the kinetic energy.

questions.stem: Why can no amount of work accelerate a proton to the speed of light?
options: Its rest mass would shrink to zero as its speed came close to c
Length contraction would make the accelerator too short to use
Time dilation would stop its clock, so it could not accelerate
Its kinetic energy, (γ − 1)mc², would become infinite as v reached c
questions.explanation: As v approaches c, γ grows without limit, so the energy needed to go faster grows without limit too. Any finite amount of work leaves the proton just below c. Its rest mass does not change with speed.

questions.stem: A proton’s total energy is 3.0 times its rest energy. What is its speed?
questions.explanation: Total energy γmc² = 3.0mc² gives γ = 3.0, so 1 − v²/c² = 1/9 and v = √(8/9) c ≈ 0.94c. 0.89c forgets the square root, and 0.33c is 1/γ.

questions.stem: At what speed is a particle’s kinetic energy equal to its rest energy?
questions.explanation: Ek = (γ − 1)mc² equals mc² when γ = 2. Then 1 − v²/c² = 1/4, so v = √(3/4) c ≈ 0.87c. 0.75c forgets the square root, and 0.50c is 1/γ.

questions.stem: The Sun radiates energy at about 3.8 × 10²⁶ W. By about how much does its mass decrease each second? Use c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
options: 1.3 × 10¹⁸ kg
3.4 × 10⁴³ kg
questions.explanation: Each second the Sun releases 3.8 × 10²⁶ J, so Δm = E/c² = 3.8 × 10²⁶/(3.0 × 10⁸)² ≈ 4.2 × 10⁹ kg. Dividing by c only once gives 1.3 × 10¹⁸ kg, and multiplying by c² gives an impossibly large 3.4 × 10⁴³ kg.

questions.stem: In fusion in the Sun’s core, how does the total mass of the products compare with the total mass of the reactants?
options: It is far less; most of the reactants’ mass is turned into sunlight
It is slightly less; the missing mass is released as energy, E = Δmc²
It is slightly more; the extra mass stores the energy that is released
It is equal; the released energy comes only from the particles’ motion
questions.explanation: The products have slightly less rest mass than the reactants, and that mass difference appears as released energy, E = Δmc². Only a small fraction of the mass, under 1%, is converted, which is why the Sun can shine for billions of years.

questions.stem: An electron and a positron, both almost at rest, annihilate. Each has a rest energy of 8.2 × 10⁻¹⁴ J. How much energy is released in total?
questions.explanation: Both particles’ rest mass is converted to energy, so the total is 2 × 8.2 × 10⁻¹⁴ ≈ 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ J, carried away by gamma-ray photons. 8.2 × 10⁻¹⁴ J counts only one of the two particles.

questions.stem: When a slow-moving electron–positron pair annihilates, two gamma-ray photons of equal energy are produced. What is the energy of each photon in electron-volts? Use electron rest energy 8.2 × 10⁻¹⁴ J and e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
questions.explanation: The total energy, 2 × 8.2 × 10⁻¹⁴ J, is shared equally, so each photon carries 8.2 × 10⁻¹⁴ J, which is 8.2 × 10⁻¹⁴/1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ ≈ 5.1 × 10⁵ eV. 1.0 × 10⁶ eV is the total for both photons, and 8.2 × 10⁻¹⁴ is the joule value labelled as eV.

questions.stem: Colliding protons in a particle accelerator can produce new particles with more total rest mass than the two protons had. Where does the extra rest mass come from?
options: The accelerator’s magnetic field energy is converted into matter
The protons’ electric charge is converted into the new mass
The protons’ kinetic energy is converted into rest mass energy
Mass is created from nothing whenever particles travel near c
questions.explanation: Mass and energy are interchangeable through E = mc². The protons’ large kinetic energy can be converted into the rest energy of new particles, while total energy is conserved. Charge is also conserved, so it cannot be turned into mass.
